content:
The lawsuit alleging Apple and OpenAI stole trade secrets continues to heat up, with OpenAI today filing a motion asking a federal judge to dismiss the case. OpenAI said Apple's complaint was filed "without adequate investigation" and took its "ordinary business activities" out of context.

Meanwhile, Apple is actively pushing for a temporary restraining order, with a hearing scheduled for October 1 in court. The entire case could take years to resolve.

In its motion to dismiss, OpenAI is attempting to get the entire case thrown out at an early stage. OpenAI argues that Apple has failed to meet legal standards, failing to demonstrate that it possesses specific trade secrets or to plausibly allege any wrongdoing.

OpenAI pointed out that the examples Apple cited of former employees discussing confidential information distort the facts. These involve iMessage conversation content that OpenAI had also published on its website earlier this week.

OpenAI said these messages show that one of the individuals named in the original complaint, Chang Liu, obtained the information at the request of an Apple employee, rather than acting in OpenAI's interest. OpenAI pointed out that Apple "does not allege that Mr. Liu disclosed any documents to OpenAI, or used any documents in OpenAI's hardware work."

Similarly, the motion to dismiss also responds to Apple's claims about a former Apple vice president, Tang Tan, retaining a document describing Apple's offboarding procedures.

Apple claimed Tan used the document to help circumvent security checks in recruiting Apple employees. In its motion today, OpenAI interpreted the matter from the opposite angle, suggesting that Tan used the information to ensure that his newly hired employees strictly followed Apple's offboarding procedures to prevent any wrongdoing.

Of course, all this legal terminology is a common litigation tactic. We still don't know whether OpenAI's arguments for dismissal meet the legal standards required, but we are not surprised by their attempt to throw out the complaint—that is exactly what lawyers are supposed to do.

At least for now, neither OpenAI nor Apple appears interested in settling the case. The next major development will most likely be the temporary restraining order hearing on October 1.
